mcqs.question: Why can't you simply use plain constructor-based dependency injection for an Activity the way you would for an ordinary Kotlin class?
options: Activities are instantiated by the Android framework, not by your own code, so there's no constructor call site you write to pass dependencies into
Activities cannot have constructors in Kotlin
Constructor injection is technically impossible in the JVM
Manual DI requires XML configuration files that Activities don't support
mcqs.explanation: The framework calls the Activity's constructor when launching it from an Intent, not your own code, so there's no ordinary call site available to pass dependencies in — this is the specific structural reason manual constructor DI doesn't work for framework-instantiated classes, and exactly what Hilt's annotation-based injection works around.

mcqs.question: A team needs Hilt to provide a Retrofit client instance. Why can't they just add @Inject to Retrofit's constructor?
options: Retrofit is a third-party class whose constructor you don't control, so Hilt needs a @Module with @Provides to be told explicitly how to build it
@Inject only works on classes with no constructor parameters
Retrofit clients cannot be injected by any DI framework
@Inject is reserved exclusively for ViewModel classes
mcqs.explanation: @Inject constructor works for classes you own and can annotate directly — a third-party class like Retrofit has no constructor you can add annotations to, so a @Module with @Provides is needed to explicitly describe how to build it, which is exactly the split between the two annotation styles.

mcqs.question: A database connection pool is injected with no scope annotation, and a new instance is created every time it's injected across the app. What's the concrete problem?
options: Nothing — unscoped is always the safest default for any dependency
This will cause a compile-time circular dependency error
Unscoped dependencies automatically default to Activity scope
This wastes resources and duplicates connections, since a database connection pool is meant to be one shared resource across the app, which is exactly the case @Singleton scoping is for
mcqs.explanation: Without a scope annotation, Hilt creates a fresh instance per injection point by default — for something genuinely meant to be one shared resource, like a connection pool, that wastes resources and can create redundant connections; @Singleton scoping ensures the same instance is reused everywhere.

mcqs.question: Is Hilt a replacement for Dagger, or built on top of it?
options: Hilt is built on top of Dagger, wrapping its dependency-resolution engine with Android-specific conventions and a standard component hierarchy
Hilt fully replaces Dagger and shares no code with it
Dagger is deprecated and Hilt is now the only supported engine
Hilt and Dagger are unrelated, competing frameworks
mcqs.explanation: Hilt uses Dagger's actual dependency-resolution engine underneath, adding Android-specific conventions (a standard component hierarchy matching Activity/Fragment/ViewModel) so most apps don't need to design their own component graph the way raw Dagger requires — it's a layer on top, not a separate engine.

mcqs.question: An Application-scoped singleton holds a listener registered by an Activity-scoped object, and never unregisters it. What's the risk, and how does it resemble a different bug covered elsewhere?
options: There is no risk since Hilt automatically unregisters listeners on scope teardown

This risks leaking the Activity the same way a static field holding a Context does — the longer-lived singleton keeps a reference tied to a shorter-lived Activity's lifetime, preventing garbage collection after the Activity is destroyed
This will fail to compile since Hilt disallows any cross-scope listener registration
The listener will simply stop firing after the Activity is destroyed with no other consequence
mcqs.explanation: Hilt's compiler catches the most direct scope violations, but a listener held indirectly by a longer-lived singleton can slip through and produce the same Context-leak pattern as a static field holding an Activity reference — the fix is the same principle: never let something longer-lived hold a standing reference to something scoped shorter than itself.

mcqs.question: Class A's constructor requires a B, and class B's constructor requires an A. What does Hilt do, and what's the recommended fix?
options: Hilt lazily initializes one of them at runtime to break the cycle automatically
Circular dependencies are only a runtime issue, not something Hilt detects
Hilt silently picks an arbitrary initialization order and hopes it works

Hilt fails at compile time with a dependency-cycle error, and the recommended fix is refactoring — extracting the shared responsibility into a third class, or replacing the direct reference with an event/callback pattern
mcqs.explanation: Hilt cannot construct either class first since each needs an already-built instance of the other, so it fails loudly at compile time rather than silently working around it — the right fix is treating this as a design smell and refactoring, not finding a way to force the cycle to resolve.
